title: Kelvin-Wave Multiplication by Sound Emission
abstract: A subsonic Kelvin quantum can emit a phonon and split into two softer quanta, increasing Kelvin population while losing energy. In the soft-phonon limit, rotational invariance relates the leading acoustic shear amplitude, odd under reversal of phonon axial momentum, to the energy released. Microscopic calculations support this dispersion dependence. In a reflecting cavity with coherent sound and Kelvin seeds, Gross--Pitaevskii evolution shows Kelvin gain, larger mean-square displacement and smaller mean-square slope; a $π$ shift of the initial sound phase reverses these changes.
summary: This paper analyzes the process where a Kelvin wave on a quantum vortex splits by emitting a sound phonon, leading to an increase in Kelvin wave population. Using the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, the authors show that this multiplication process is dynamically significant and that the resulting population gain is robust against initial phase variations. The work provides deep insights into the nonlinear coupling between quantized excitations and the bulk sound continuum in superfluids.
main_problem: The paper investigates the nonlinear process of Kelvin-Wave Multiplication by Sound Emission in superfluid quantum vortices.
main_result: The splitting channel ($K_k 	o K_{k1} + K_{k2} + B_{+1}$) is dynamically appreciable, and the mean gain of the Kelvin population survives averaging over the initial sound phase.
method: The analysis employs the Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) evolution equation, supplemented by microscopic calculations and Hamiltonian modeling to track energy and momentum transfer.
model_or_system: The system models a superfluid quantum vortex, governed by the GP equation. The dynamics involve coupling between Kelvin waves, sound modes, and the background vortex state.
key_observables: Kelvin population ($K_b$), quadratic Kelvin energy ($E_b$), mean-square displacement ($	ext{Wcore}$), and mean-square slope ($	ext{Score}$).
important_parameters: Subsonic sound velocity, initial sound phase ($\phi(0)$ vs. $\phi(0)+\pi$), and the wave number spectrum of excitations.
main_assumptions: The derivation of the leading shear coefficient neglects axial recoil, and the analysis relies on spectral assumptions for the modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the radiative processes (annihilation and splitting) on a vortex, comparing GP matrix elements to theoretical estimates, and showing the reversal of population transfer upon a $\pi$ shift of the initial sound phase.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the physical process (splitting/annihilation) to developing theoretical relations (rotational invariance, angular momentum balance), and finally validating these concepts through detailed GP simulations and microscopic rate calculations.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed, quantitative study of nonlinear wave interactions (wave multiplication) within a topological defect (vortex) in a quantum fluid, linking spectral properties to macroscopic observable changes like population growth and geometric deformation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Two radiative processes on the same vortex. Coun- terpropagating Kelvin quanta annihilate into m = −2 sound. Splitting leaves two softer quanta and emits m = +1 sound, whose positive angular momentum permits an increase of Kelvin number. The curves indicate displacement modes, not separate vortices.

FIG. 2. Dispersion constraint and coherent Kelvin conversion. (a) Reduced shear coefficient ΛGP odd from microscopic GP matrix elements at q/p = ±0.5 (symbols; definition in Supplemental Material), compared with ΛE = ∆E0/[2α0(1−α0)k2] (solid lines). The dashed estimate EK(k)/k2 uses only the parent dispersion. (b) Population of all retained bound Kelvin modes: GP symbols and independent three-mode predictions for initial sound phases ϕ(0) B and ϕ(0) B + π. Gray triangles show ⟨Kb(t)⟩ϕB/⟨Kb(0)⟩ϕB with equal weights for eight initial phases; the gray line is the corresponding phase-averaged three-mode prediction.

FIG. 3. Vortex geometry in the same two GP evolutions as Fig. 2(b). (a) Mean-square displacement of the instantaneous vortex zero. (b) Mean-square slope. Both quantities are normalized to their own values at t = 0. The curves retain the preparation transient and fast oscillations; no time average or sound subtraction is applied. The initial sound phase reverses both geometrical trends.
